clinical_category: Oncology psychosocial care - guilt and self-blame
stem: A cancer survivor tells the nurse, 'I keep blaming myself for choices I made before I got cancer. I feel so guilty that I have stopped talking to my friends about what I am going through.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Acknowledge the guilt without reinforcing self-blame, explore how it is affecting coping and relationships, and offer counseling or support resources if the feelings are difficult to manage.
options.B: Tell the client that guilt is useful because self-blame is necessary to prevent cancer from recurring.
options.C: Avoid discussing the guilt because emotional reactions after cancer treatment have little relevance to survivorship care.
options.D: Explain that withdrawing from friends is the healthiest way to manage guilt until the feeling disappears on its own.

rationale: A is correct. NCI states that many people with cancer experience guilt and may blame themselves for lifestyle choices they believe contributed to cancer. NCI advises that having cancer is not the person's fault and recommends sharing feelings with trusted people, counselors, support groups, or the healthcare team. NCI also recognizes guilt/self-blame and avoidance of people as possible cancer-related post-traumatic stress symptoms, so persistent or disruptive distress warrants assessment and support. B reinforces unsupported causal blame and incorrectly links guilt with recurrence prevention. C dismisses a recognized psychosocial need. D promotes isolation even though NCI identifies social and professional support as potential coping resources.
educational_objective: Respond therapeutically to cancer-related guilt and self-blame by assessing its effect on coping and relationships, avoiding reinforcement of blame, and facilitating appropriate emotional and social support.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Emotions and Cancer; Cancer-Related Post-Traumatic Stress (PDQ®)
source_locator: Emotions and Cancer — heading 'Guilt' and 'More Ways to Cope with Your Emotions' → 'Express your feelings' and 'Don't blame yourself for your cancer'; Cancer-Related Post-Traumatic Stress PDQ — symptom list including guilt/self-blame and avoiding people, plus treatment section supporting counseling and support groups.
source_claim_supported: NCI recognizes cancer-related guilt and self-blame, advises against blaming oneself for cancer, supports expression of feelings and counseling/support-group resources, and identifies guilt/self-blame and social avoidance among possible cancer-related stress symptoms.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Client Needs category 'Psychosocial Integrity' — nursing care that promotes emotional, mental and social well-being; applied here to coping, self-concept, therapeutic communication and social/professional support.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's narrowly framed survivor-guilt recognition item into a directly NCI-supported guilt/self-blame scenario. Removed the unsupported implication that guilt necessarily arises from outliving other patients and removed any causal claim that guilt itself produces withdrawal.
audit_findings: Fresh NCI review directly supports guilt and self-blame as cancer-related emotional experiences and explicitly advises against assuming personal fault for developing cancer.
NCI supports sharing feelings with trusted people, counseling and support groups when emotional distress is difficult to manage.
The source item was rebuilt because the exact survivor-guilt formulation was less directly supported by authoritative current guidance than general cancer-related guilt/self-blame.
The rationale now avoids claiming that guilt causes social withdrawal; it treats the client's stated withdrawal as a separate sign of coping difficulty requiring assessment.
Independent adversarial review found no second answer, cueing, stigmatizing causal claim, locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or unresolved conflict.
